title: Brilliant Genius!
reviewNotes: Three branches from stable six-piece position after Rxe4 at 103 seconds. Black to move, Kc1, b2/c5 versus Ka3 Re4 c4. b1=N+ forces king moves permitting Nc3+ or Nd2+ forks; independent legal retreat/capture completions explicitly labeled. Queen promotion instead loses to independently completed Re1+ skewer. Earlier larger bishop sacrifice remains source context.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players will accept a draw, but only a true genius would be able to find the incredible win that black has in this position. The black bishop [music] is hanging and white is about to get a new queen, but after B7, black creates a threat of getting his own queen. And so now promoting would not [music] be good enough. White has to spend the move playing rook to H7 trying to come [music] around and stop the promotion to the black queen. Now if black was to promote, of course after rook to H1, black would be forced to give up the queen, give up the bishop, and [music] this would be a win for white. But black is not that naive, and he prevents the rook from going to H1. After bishop takes [music] G2, now the bishop defends that square, and it is not easy for the rook to recreate the threat. Taking here [music] would still be stopped by the bishop, but white has fighting spirit, and he finds a brilliant idea. He now promotes to the queen. [music] Of course, this move is trying to distract the bishop from the defense of the F1 square, and the bishop has to oblige. Now after rook takes F7, the threat of coming to the eighth rank and securing the king seems unstoppable. The bishop can come back for a moment, [music] but after rook to E7, it is impossible to defend this dark square with a light square bishop. And if the king comes to defend, of course we would lose this pawn, and this is actually completely winning for white. So is this it? Is black stuck in the woods? Well, black plays on. And he plays a mysterious move. Bishop to E4. A move that looks like a mouse slip. Isn't this just a complete blunder of the bishop? This doesn't change anything. Black cannot get a queen because of this skewer, but you see black had foreseen from afar that in this position he could win the game by promoting to a knight. What? How can a knight win against [music] a rook? Well, usually it can't. But notice that no matter where this king steps, there is always going to be a knight fork that will pick up the rook. And not only that, after one of these forks, the knight is also going to very conveniently defend the pawn, >> [music] >> which means that black can start walking the king and win the game. If you love incredible chess, follow for more.
